result:
This looks good. The file is self-contained, uses JUnit 3.8-style `TestCase`/`assert*`/`fail` matching the rest of the project, avoids Java 1.6-incompatible syntax, and covers happy paths, boundary cases (multi-digit indices, empty registry), and error cases (malformed patterns, disabled mutators).

## Summary

Added `src/test/org/apache/commons/lang/text/ExtendedMessageFormatAgentTest.java` (JUnit 3.8 style, matching the rest of the project). 22 tests run, 21 pass, 1 fails — and that failure exposes a real bug:

**`testAppendQuotedStringAdvancesPastLeadingQuote`** — shows a bug in `ExtendedMessageFormat.appendQuotedString`. Its leading check (`if (escapingOn && c[start] == QUOTE) return appendTo.append(QUOTE);`) fires unconditionally whenever it's called the way `applyPattern()` calls it (positioned exactly on the opening quote), so it returns immediately without ever advancing the parse position or consuming the quoted text. The consequence at the integration level (not run directly in the suite, since it would hang/OOM the JVM — noted in a comment instead) is that **any pattern containing a single quote character, combined with a non-null format registry, makes `applyPattern()` spin forever**, appending the quote character to its buffer until the heap is exhausted. The reflection-based test isolates this root cause safely and deterministically.

Two of my initial test assumptions turned out to be wrong rather than bugs, and I corrected them instead of keeping false failures: a null pattern throws `NullPointerException` (inherited from `java.text.MessageFormat`, not a defect specific to this class), and an unterminated quote with no registry is tolerated by the JDK's `MessageFormat` (treated as running to end-of-string) rather than rejected.
